Cold gas efficiency and effective thermal efficiency 86 COMPARISON OF COMMERCIAL, STATE-OF-THE-ART, FOSSIL-BASED AMMONIA PRODUCTION Exhibit 4-3 shows a metric for net energy consumption of ammonia plants, which considers natural gas input and electricity input, normalized by ammonia production (first presented in Section 2.13.3) (Tavares, et al., 2013). The lowest net energy consumption is 27.7 GJ/tonne NH 3 for the non-capture case, Case 1, as expected. The highest net energy consumption is 29.2 GJ/tonne NH for Case 2. Adding capture to Case 1 increases net energy consumption of the 3 plant by 5.5 percent. The net energy consumption metric is useful for comparing with data from technology suppliers and to see historically how energy consumption has decreased over time for ammonia production facilities. For example, energy consumption has dropped from 62 GJ/tonne in the 1950s to 28 GJ/tonne in current plants (Kermeli, et al., 2017). As of 2011, the Haldor Topsoe process and Uhde process report net energy consumption of 27.9 GJ/tonne and 27.0 GJ/tonne, respectively (Kermeli, et al., 2017). For various ammonia technology suppliers, net energy consumption ranges from as high as 32.8 GJ/tonne NH (for the Humphreys and 3 Glasgow Process when CO is recovered) to as low as 26.8 GJ/tonne NH (for the Jacobs Plus 2 3 Ammonia Technology when steam is exported) (Kermeli, et al., 2017). Overall, the net energy consumption of the study cases are within the range reported by ammonia technology suppliers. Exhibit 4-3.
